messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marcus was twenty-four when his girlfriend Jenna came home drunk, the sour smell of whiskey billowing off her breath. She had always been volatile, but that night she was a different person. She accused him of things he hadn't done, and when he tried to calm her, she swung. He still remembers the sound of his own head hitting the tile, the metallic taste of blood, and her voice screaming something he could never quite make out. The visible bruises on his face took weeks to fade, but the invisible ones dug deeper.

In the months afterward, he found himself reacting to things that had never bothered him before. The first time he caught the faintest whiff of alcohol on a witness during an interrogation, his stomach lurched into nausea and the memory of Jenna’s shouts filled his ears—vivid, uninvited, unmistakable. That moment, standing there trying to look professional, he felt something crack inside: he no longer believed people were good. Anyone could flip. Anyone could hurt him. The nausea and the smell became a direct line to that belief, and he started seeing danger everywhere. As a detective, he encountered wounded bodies daily, and every visible injury on a victim sent him reeling back to his own battered face, reinforcing his sense that he was permanently separate from the innocent world.

His distrust grew into a quiet certainty that others were not what they seemed, and that certainty would not let the memory rest. He replayed the night over and over, trying to find the moment he should have left, the sign he missed. The memory was so clear—the sound of her voice, the pattern of the floor tiles—that it felt like a recording he could not stop. To keep it from overwhelming him, he started numbing his emotions. He avoided relaxing because stillness felt like an open door to the past. He avoided physical contact entirely, even flinching when his wife Sarah reached for his hand across the dinner table. He told himself it was just a habit, but the numbness spread, and soon he felt like a stranger in his own marriage.

The irony was that his very attempts to stay safe made everything worse. By refusing to let his guard down, he became hypervigilant to every possible trigger: the sudden onset of nausea, the glimpse of a scar on someone else’s skin, the faintest trace of alcohol at a work event. Each time he tensed, he felt his alienation deepen, and the memory of Jenna roared back with fresh intensity. He was caught in a loop he could not name. Sarah tried to talk to him, but he dismissed her concerns, certain she could not understand. The only thing that made him feel in control was staying busy, staying distracted, staying untouched.

It was after a case where he had to photograph a woman’s facial fractures that he came home, showered, and sat on the edge of the bed unable to move. Sarah sat beside him and did not touch him. That night, he admitted he needed help. He was terrified of what it would mean to let the memories surface without his walls up, but he was more afraid of losing the one person who still reached for him.
